trans-unit.source: Visitors audit their own website: crawl, technical SEO, content, performance and security. Limited tests per day.
Enter your URL and get a detailed SEO report within minutes: up to %1$s pages are crawled, more than 60 checks on indexing, content, performance, structured data and security, with clear priorities.
You have used your %1$s free tests for today. New tests are available tomorrow.
Only publicly accessible pages are fetched. Reports are available via their link for 30 days.
For Core Web Vitals the start URL is sent to Google PageSpeed Insights.
Not just meta tags: the checker crawls your site like a search engine and evaluates every finding by its impact.
Enter the address of your website – no registration needed.
We analyse robots.txt, sitemaps and up to %1$s pages and check their links.
You get a report with score, priorities and concrete recommendations.
Can search engines reach, crawl and index your pages?
HTTPS, redirects, robots.txt, XML sitemaps, canonicals, noindex, broken links, soft 404
Do titles, descriptions, headings and content describe your pages well?
Titles, meta descriptions, headings, duplicates, content length, alt texts, link texts, language
How fast and mobile-friendly is the site?
Core Web Vitals, server response, compression, HTTP/2, caching, render-blocking resources, images, viewport
Can search engines and social networks understand and present your content?
Schema.org/JSON-LD, Open Graph, Twitter Cards, favicon, hreflang
TLS certificate, HSTS, mixed content, security headers
Please keep this page open – the analysis usually takes one to three minutes. You can bookmark the link and come back later.
The findings with the biggest expected impact – start here.
Very good – only minor improvements left.
Solid foundation with clear potential for improvement.
Significant issues – they can noticeably limit visibility.

Each check has a weight from 1 to 10. Passed checks count fully, warnings half, errors not at all; notes are not scored. Page-level checks only become errors when a relevant share of pages is affected. The categories are weighted (indexing 30 %, content 25 %, performance 20 %, structured data 15 %, security 10 %). The score shows how well established best practices are met – it is not a prediction of rankings.
Up to %1$s pages are crawled per test, starting at the home page and complemented by a sample from the XML sitemap. robots.txt rules are respected.

Limits: pages are analysed as delivered HTML; content that only appears after JavaScript execution is not evaluated. Length recommendations for titles and descriptions are guidelines – Google does not publish fixed limits. Core Web Vitals come from Google PageSpeed Insights (field data where available).

HTTPS is a confirmed Google ranking signal and a precondition for trust. Browsers mark HTTP pages as "not secure".

Requests via http:// should be redirected permanently (301 or 308) to https://, so that only one version is indexed and link signals are consolidated.

The site is not served on http:// at all – that is fine.
Both host variants should not deliver content. The secondary variant should permanently redirect to the main host, otherwise duplicate content is created.
%1$s delivers content itself instead of redirecting to %2$s.
The variant %1$s is not in use.
Every redirect costs loading time and crawl budget. Link directly to the final URL and avoid chains of several hops.
The entered URL loads without redirect.

The robots.txt controls which areas crawlers may access. A server error (5xx) causes Google to pause crawling; "Disallow: /" blocks the whole site.
robots.txt is present and does not block the site.
No robots.txt found (status %1$s). Crawling is allowed, but a file with a sitemap reference is recommended.
robots.txt returns a server error (%1$s) – Google may stop crawling.
robots.txt blocks the entire website for search engines.
A "Sitemap:" line in robots.txt helps all search engines find your XML sitemap.
robots.txt does not reference a sitemap.
%1$s sitemap URL(s) referenced in robots.txt cannot be loaded as a valid sitemap – check the address.
An XML sitemap lists all indexable URLs and helps search engines find new and changed pages quickly. Sitemap index files are followed.
The sitemap could not be read as valid XML.
A sitemap should only contain indexable URLs with status 200: no redirects, errors, noindex pages or URLs whose canonical points elsewhere.
No sitemap URLs were part of the crawl sample.
Pages with "noindex" (meta robots or X-Robots-Tag header) do not appear in search results. This is correct for e.g. legal notices or internal search, but often happens by mistake after a relaunch.
The start page is set to noindex and will not appear in search results.
Pages with 4xx or 5xx status are not indexed and frustrate visitors. Server errors (5xx) can also slow down crawling of the whole site.
Internal links to missing pages waste crawl budget, lose link signals and lead visitors into dead ends. The list shows the target and where it is linked.
No broken internal links found (%2$s checked).
%1$s broken internal link targets found (%2$s checked).
Links to pages that no longer exist harm user experience and look neglected. Sites that block bots (401, 403, 429) are not counted as broken.
No broken external links found (%2$s checked).
Internal links should point directly to the final URL. Links via redirects cost loading time and crawl budget – typical causes are missing trailing slashes or old URLs.
Internal links point directly to their targets.
A self-referencing canonical tag tells search engines the preferred URL and protects against duplicates caused by parameters or variants.
Canonicals should be absolute, unique and point to an indexable page with status 200 on the same host. Contradictory canonicals are ignored by Google.
A non-existent URL must return status 404 or 410. If it returns 200 ("soft 404"), search engines may index error pages; redirecting everything to the home page is also treated as soft 404.
A non-existent URL returns status %1$s instead of 404.
Missing pages are redirected to the start page.
Short, lower-case URLs with hyphens are easier to read and share. Upper case, underscores, very long URLs and many parameters favour duplicates.
Meta refresh redirects are slow and not accessible. Use server-side 301 redirects instead.
Google can render JavaScript, but with delay and not always completely; other search engines and AI crawlers often cannot. Important content should be in the delivered HTML (server-side rendering).
The start page delivers only %1$s words of text without JavaScript – content is probably rendered client-side.
The main content is contained in the delivered HTML.
Whether AI assistants may use your content is a business decision. Blocking them can reduce visibility in AI answers; allowing them makes your content available for training and answers.
No AI crawler is blocked completely.
llms.txt is an optional, not yet standardised proposal to give AI systems a structured overview of a website. It has no influence on Google rankings.
The title is one of the most important on-page signals and usually appears as the headline in search results. Every page needs exactly one unique <title>.
Titles of roughly 25–65 characters are usually displayed in full. Google does not publish a fixed limit – it truncates by pixel width. Put the most important terms at the beginning.
Identical titles make it hard for search engines to tell pages apart and lead to competing pages. Each page should have its own descriptive title.
The meta description is not a ranking factor, but Google often uses it as the snippet. A good description increases the click-through rate.
Around 70–170 characters is a good guideline. Google has no fixed maximum and may rewrite the snippet anyway – what matters is a precise, appealing summary.
Identical descriptions on many pages are usually ignored by Google. Write individual descriptions at least for important pages.
The H1 names the topic of the page for visitors and search engines. Each page should have a meaningful main heading.
Several H1s are technically allowed, but one clear main heading makes the structure easier to understand – also for screen readers.
Headings should be nested without skipping levels (H1 → H2 → H3). A clean outline helps search engines and assistive technologies.
The same H1 on several pages indicates template headings or near-duplicate pages.
There is no minimum word count for rankings. Very short pages (under 150 words of main content), however, often do not answer the search intent sufficiently. Navigation and footer are not counted.
Pages with identical main content compete with each other. Merge them, differentiate the content or set a canonical to the preferred version.
Alt texts describe images for screen readers and image search. Images without an alt attribute are counted; alt="" for purely decorative images is correct and not penalised.
All %2$s images have an alt attribute.
%1$s of %2$s images have no alt attribute.
If an image is the only content of a link, its alt text is the link text. An empty alt makes the link unnamed for screen readers and search engines.
Descriptive link texts help users and search engines understand the target. Avoid empty links and phrases like "click here" or "read more".
The lang attribute on <html> (e.g. "de" or "en-GB") helps browsers, screen readers and search engines identify the language.
Topic focus of the start page
Compares the most frequent terms in the main content with title and H1. This is only an indication: title and content should clearly address the same topic.
Frequent terms: %1$s – none of them appears in title or H1.
Google Lighthouse lab test on a simulated mid-range smartphone. It is a diagnostic value; for rankings the Core Web Vitals of real users count.
PageSpeed data could not be retrieved this time.
How quickly the largest visible element loads. Good: up to 2.5 s. Optimise server response, hero image (size, format, preload) and render-blocking resources.
%1$s (lab value – not enough field data available).
How quickly the page reacts to clicks and input. Good: up to 200 ms. Reduce long JavaScript tasks and third-party scripts.
%1$s (lab value – not enough field data available).
How much the layout shifts while loading. Good: up to 0.1. Reserve space for images, ads and embeds (width/height) and avoid late-loading fonts and banners.
%1$s (lab value – not enough field data available).
Lab metric for how long the main thread is blocked by JavaScript; a good indicator for INP. Good: up to 200 ms.
Time to first byte measured from our server. Below 600 ms is good. Slow responses delay every other metric – use caching, faster hosting or a CDN.
Very large HTML documents (over 400 KB) load and render slowly, often because of inline data, SVGs or page builders.
Text compression typically reduces HTML, CSS and JS by 70–90 %. It is enabled with one server setting.
Modern protocols load many resources in parallel over one connection and noticeably reduce loading times.
CSS, JavaScript and images should be cacheable for a long time (Cache-Control max-age of at least 7 days, ideally a year with versioned file names).
Sampled resources are cached long enough.
%1$s of %2$s sampled resources have no or a short cache lifetime.
Scripts in <head> without async or defer block rendering of the page. Load them with defer or at the end of the body.
%1$s blocking script(s) in <head> of the start page.
Every file means additional requests and parsing. Bundle files and remove unused libraries and third-party tools.
%1$s files on the start page (%2$s scripts, %3$s stylesheets).
Images without width and height attributes cause layout shifts (CLS) because the browser cannot reserve space in advance.
Images outside the visible area should be loaded with loading="lazy". Do not lazy-load the main image at the top (LCP).
WebP and AVIF are usually 25–50 % smaller than JPEG/PNG at the same quality. Deliver them e.g. via <picture> or srcset.
%1$s %% of the raster images use WebP/AVIF (%2$s of %3$s).
Too few images for an assessment.
More than about 1,500 elements slow down rendering and interactions, especially on smartphones.
Google indexes the mobile version (mobile-first). A viewport meta tag with width=device-width is required; zooming should not be disabled.
<!DOCTYPE html> prevents quirks mode, a declared charset (UTF-8) prevents broken umlauts and special characters.
Schema.org markup (ideally JSON-LD) helps search engines understand content and enables rich results such as breadcrumbs, FAQs, reviews or events.
Faulty JSON is ignored completely; missing required properties prevent rich results. Validate with Google's Rich Results Test.
Organization, LocalBusiness or Person markup with name, logo and contact details supports the knowledge panel and brand recognition.
Organization, business or person markup found.
No Organization, LocalBusiness or Person markup found.
og:title, og:description and og:image (absolute URL) control how pages look when shared on LinkedIn, Facebook, WhatsApp & co.
A twitter:card tag (e.g. summary_large_image) enables large preview images on X. Without it, X falls back to Open Graph.
Google shows the favicon next to the result on mobile. It should be at least 48×48 px and crawlable.

For multilingual sites, hreflang links language versions. Each version must reference itself and all others (return links), use valid codes (e.g. de, en-GB) and absolute URLs; x-default is recommended.
No hreflang – fine for single-language websites.
Pages in several languages (%1$s) found, but no hreflang.
An expired certificate makes the site inaccessible for visitors and search engines. Automate renewal (e.g. Let's Encrypt).
Strict-Transport-Security forces browsers to always use HTTPS and prevents downgrade attacks. Recommended: max-age of at least six months.
HSTS is active, but only for %1$s days.
Resources loaded via http:// on HTTPS pages are blocked by browsers or trigger warnings. Load all resources via https://.
Security headers protect visitors against clickjacking, MIME sniffing and data leakage. They are not a direct ranking factor, but a sign of a well-maintained website.
Version numbers in Server or X-Powered-By headers make targeted attacks easier. Remove them in the server configuration.
